title: Kotlin services on the JVM
description: For a Kotlin service on the JVM: coroutine scopes, null boundaries with Java, compiler warnings, style and static analysis, and pinned Gradle dependencies. It leaves out what other packs own: a Kotlin service on Spring Boot keeps `spring-boot`, an Android app keeps `android-app`.

sources.title: Kotlin documentation, calling Java from Kotlin
Kotlin documentation, code quality tools in Kotlin projects

rules.instruction: Start every coroutine from a scope that something owns and cancels: `coroutineScope` inside the suspending function that needs concurrent work, or the Ktor `Application` scope, which is cancelled when the application stops, for background work that lives as long as the service. Do not use `GlobalScope`, and do not build a `CoroutineScope()` at the call site to replace it.
rules.verification: Search the main sources for `GlobalScope` and for `CoroutineScope(` and replace each hit. In a test, cancel the owning scope or stop the application and check that the work it launched has stopped.

rules.instruction: When Kotlin code receives a value from a Java API or library, declare the Kotlin type of the variable, property or function result yourself, so that no platform type is inferred: `String?` when the Java side can return null, `String` only when its contract rules null out. A Java declaration with a nullability annotation Kotlin reads needs no declaration of yours.
rules.verification: For each Java call in the change, read the receiving declaration for an explicit type, then run a test that makes the Java side return null where it can: the code must handle the null or fail at that boundary with a clear message, not later with a `NullPointerException`.

rules.instruction: Set `allWarningsAsErrors` to true in the Kotlin `compilerOptions`, for the whole project or in the shared convention plugin of the modules, and fix a warning instead of hiding it: leave `suppressWarnings` at false.
rules.verification: Add an unused variable on a scratch branch and check that `./gradlew compileKotlin` fails, then check that every module applies the option. task verify looks for it in the Gradle files; review each file it names.

rules.instruction: Apply the official Kotlin coding conventions with a formatter and a static analyzer that Gradle runs, such as ktlint and detekt, which the Kotlin documentation shows, and attach both tasks to `check` so that a violation fails the build. Record each accepted exception in the tool's own configuration with its reason.
rules.verification: On a scratch branch, break a rule of the formatter and one of the analyzer, run `./gradlew check` and read the executed tasks: both tools must run and the build must fail.

rules.instruction: Declare the versions of Kotlin, Ktor, every library and every plugin once in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` and use the type-safe accessors in build scripts (`libs.` and `alias(libs.plugins.`), with no version literal in a module's build script. Keep every Ktor artifact on one version, taken from the Ktor Gradle plugin, which adds the Ktor BOM, or from one catalog entry.
rules.verification: Search the module build scripts for quoted `group:artifact:version` strings and `version =` literals, then run `./gradlew :<module>:dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath` and check that every `io.ktor` artifact resolves to the same version.

rules.instruction: Turn on Gradle dependency locking for every configuration with `dependencyLocking { lockAllConfigurations() }`, commit `gradle.lockfile`, and change it only with `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks` (or `--update-locks` with the module names) in a commit that says why. Pin no `-SNAPSHOT` or other changing version.
rules.verification: On a scratch branch, raise a dependency version without rewriting the locks and check that the build fails. Check that `git ls-files gradle.lockfile` lists the file and that the diff of a dependency update shows the lock change.
